raw_case_text:
The patient is an 11-year-old Lebanese girl, diagnosed with aplastic anemia. She presented to our center for a second opinion and to discuss treatment with allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT). History went back to 1 month prior to presentation when the patient was found to have thrombocytopenia on a routine blood test reaching 60,000/cu.mm. Her platelet count continued to decline, along with her hemoglobin level. She received two doses of intravenous immunoglobulin therapy. Bone marrow aspirate was done and revealed the diagnosis of aplastic anemia. The patient started receiving platelet and packed red blood cell transfusions on a regular basis. Further work up was initiated to plan for a fully matched HSCT from her sister. However, the pretransplant workup showed positive direct and indirect brucella titers (1/160 each). Therefore, she was referred to the Pediatric Infectious Diseases clinic for further evaluation. Upon further questioning, the patient reported a history of headaches, myalgias and polyarticular pain of lower extremities and mid-back, associated with night-time subjective fevers, with no other complaints. There was no recalled history of ingestion of unpasteurized dairy products. Physical exam was remarkable for bilateral knee swelling. Initial blood investigations showed anemia (Hb 7.5 g/dl), leucopenia (white cell count of 2100/cu.mm with an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of 504/cu.mm), thrombocytopenia (platelet count of 9000/cu.mm) and a reticulocyte percentage of 0.3%. Her liver enzymes were mildly elevated (alanine aminotransferase 178 IU/L) with normal bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase. Lactic dehydrogenase was within normal range. The inflammatory markers were elevated including serum ferritin (1040 ng/ml), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (54 mm/h). C-reactive protein was (1.3 mg/l). The serological tests for HIV, hepatitis C virus, hepatitis B surface antigen, anti-hepatitis B core antigen, and anti-hepatitis B surface antigen were negative. The cytomegalovirus IgG and Epstein-Barr virus IgG were positive, but IgM was negative for both. Antinuclear antibody was negative. Repeated bone marrow aspirate showed a severely aplastic pattern with less than 5% cellular marrow and no evidence of malignancy. The patient was maintained on packed red blood cells (PRBC) and platelet transfusions at a frequency of every 2-3 days. Egg preservation was done as part of HSCT preparation. Blood cultures were collected for brucella assessment that showed no growth and repeated cultures were sterile. Similarly bone marrow culture for brucella was negative for any growth, however, RNA 16 S test of bone marrow aspirate came back positive with Brucella melitensis. The patient was started on oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and rifampin 600 mg once daily.
Whole body MRI showed numerous bone lesions involving the lower cervical, thoracic, and visualized lumbar spine with low signal intensity on T1, low signal intensity on T2 and faint enhancement after contrast administration. Other few scattered lesions were noted in the left femoral head, bilateral proximal femur, iliac bones and sacrum, and right ulna. Accordingly, Brucella involvement of the bone was presumed, and the patient was admitted to receive intravenous Gentamicin 2.5 mg/kg/dose every 8 h for a total of 3 weeks duration while continuing doxycycline and rifampin. During this period of time, the patient had flares of body aches, at points that correlated with lesions found on MRI, with persistent fatigue. Her hematological parameters improved gradually after treatment initiation. Her last CBCD done 5 months after her last transfusion showed a hemoglobin level of 13.7 g/dl, white cell count of 3600 /cu.mm, and platelet count of 107000 /cu.mm. The patient's diffuse bony pain improved significantly.
The treatment regimen consisted of 21 days of IV Gentamicin, along with a total of 8 months of oral doxycycline and rifampin. We observed as expected, a late platelet recovery after almost 14 months from initiation of antibiotics. On the contrary, WBC and ANC values trended up after completing 4 months of antimicrobial therapy. This is demonstrated in Fig. 1, Fig. 2 respectively. It is important to note that the need to transfuse our patient started to decrease gradually at almost 2 months post antibiotic initiation.
To our knowledge, this is the first case of a brucella infection causing aplastic anemia in Lebanon.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 11-year-old female presented with pancytopenia and transfusion dependence, accompanied by headaches, myalgias, polyarticular joint pain, back pain, and subjective night fevers.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was found to have thrombocytopenia (60,000/cu.mm) on routine blood work 1 month prior, which progressed to severe pancytopenia and transfusion dependency despite two doses of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). Bone marrow aspiration revealed severe aplastic anemia, and she was referred for allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). Review of history revealed headaches, myalgias, polyarticular lower extremity and mid-back pain, and subjective nighttime fevers. Identification of underlying chronic infection led to targeted antimicrobial therapy, leading to transfusion independence and complete hematologic recovery without stem cell transplantation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diagnosis of severe aplastic anemia 1 month prior; received two doses of IVIG; transfusion dependency requiring packed red blood cells and platelet transfusions every 2-3 days; underwent oocyte cryopreservation. Denied ingestion of unpasteurized dairy products.
subjective.review_of_systems: Headaches, myalgias, polyarticular pain in lower extremities and mid-back, and nighttime subjective fevers; denies other complaints. Home medications: None documented. Allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: Bilateral knee swelling with joint tenderness. No other focal abnormalities documented.
objective.routine_investigations: Hematology: Hb 7.5 g/dl, WBC 2,100/cu.mm (absolute neutrophil count 504/cu.mm), platelets 9,000/cu.mm, reticulocytes 0.3%. Biochemistry: ALT 178 IU/L, bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase normal, LDH normal. Inflammatory markers: Ferritin 1,040 ng/ml, ESR 54 mm/h, CRP 1.3 mg/l. Infectious and autoimmune serologies: Negative for HIV, HBV, HCV, ANA; CMV IgG and EBV IgG positive with negative IgM. Multiple blood cultures and bone marrow cultures: Sterile without bacterial growth. Hematologic follow-up: Transfusion requirements subsided at 2 months; CBC at 5 months post-transfusion showed Hb 13.7 g/dl, WBC 3,600/cu.mm, platelets 107,000/cu.mm; full platelet recovery achieved at 14 months.
objective.advanced_workup: Bone marrow aspiration: Severely aplastic marrow (<5% cellularity) with no evidence of hematologic malignancy. Whole-body MRI: Numerous diffuse osseous lesions involving lower cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine (low signal on T1, low signal on T2, faint contrast enhancement), with additional lesions in left femoral head, bilateral proximal femurs, iliac bones, sacrum, and right ulna.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Brucellosis-induced aplastic anemia and multifocal osteomyelitis, confirmed by 16S rRNA gene PCR of bone marrow aspirate positive for Brucella melitensis, and positive direct and indirect Brucella serological titers (1:160 each), despite sterile blood and bone marrow cultures.
Plan & Clinical Course: Initially started on oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and rifampin 600 mg once daily. Upon identification of extensive bone involvement on MRI, IV gentamicin 2.5 mg/kg/dose every 8 hours was added for 21 days (3 weeks). Oral doxycycline and rifampin were continued for a total duration of 8 months. Transfusion requirements ceased within 2 months; bone pain resolved; neutrophil and WBC counts normalized by 4 months, and complete platelet recovery occurred at 14 months, avoiding allogeneic HSCT.
